newsitem.title: FRANCE: LVMH seeks drinks merger with Guinness, GrandMet.
newsitem.headline: LVMH seeks drinks merger with Guinness, GrandMet.

text.p: Luxury goods company LVMH Moet Hennessy Louis Vuitton proposed Wednesday to blend its wine and spirits businesses with those of British companies Guinness Plc and Grand Metropolitan Plc in an independent, listed company.

LVMH Chairman Bernard Arnault outlined the proposal to create a global alcoholic beverage leader to the chairmen of the British groups at a meeting in Paris held to discuss his opposition to their planned merger, which was announced in May, LVMH said in a statement.

Grand Met Chairman George Bull and Guinness Chairman Tony Greener said they would consider Arnault's proposals so long as they offered more value for shareholders than their planned 24 billion- pound ($39.8 billion) merger.
Analysts said it was not clear at first glance that Guinness and Grand Met shareholders would benefit from LVMH's proposal.

But LVMH said it would "create significantly greater value for the shareholders of the three companies than the merger proposed by Guinness and Grand Met, both in terms of potential synergies and market valuation of a coherent company with a portfolio of prestige brands, clearly a leader in its market."

Moet Hennessy, LVMH's alcoholic beverage subsidiary, makes Moet & Chandon and Pommery champagnes and Hennessy cognacs. Guinness's labels include Johnny Walker and Dewar's whiskies and Gordon's Gin, and Grand Met brands include Smirnoff, J&B and Baileys.

Analysts say LVMH would hold 30 percent to 35 percent of the wine and spirits giant. They also say Arnault is fighting to keep from being marginalized in the spirits business by the Guinness-Grand Met megamerger and having his capital locked up in a subsidiary of the new spirits-to-fast-food GMG Brands.
He would have only about 10 percent of GMG Brands if the merger went through in its current form and would not even be assured a seat on the board.

The one-hour meeting of the three chairmen in Paris followed a two-pronged assault by Arnault on the British companies. In the past two weeks, LVMH has spent more than 8 billion francs ($1.4 billion) to buy 6.4 percent of Grand Met in an apparent bid to line up votes to block the merger.

LVMH had previously taken legal action against Guinness, in which it holds 14.2 percent, to force the company to shed its stakes in their valuable joint distribution ventures. Those ventures hold the rights for 10 years to market Guinness brands in France, the United States and much of the Far East.
Financial analysts said Arnault looks like a credible threat but needs to prove his plan would create more value for Guinness and Grand Met shareholders than the companies' planned merger.

After the meeting, the British chairmen said in a joint statement, "We have made it clear to Mr .Arnault that we are, of course, open to any proposals provided that they create additional value for our shareholders beyond our existing proposal and that this is fairly shared between them."
